analysis.one_liner: Cuts business tax rates to 10% for companies that raise pay and provide health and retirement benefits, and lets firms bring foreign profits home at 5%
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let corporations — and owners of partnerships, S corporations, and sole proprietorships — pay a 10% tax rate instead of the up-to-35% rates then in effect, and would let companies bring foreign profits back to the U.S. taxed at only 5%. The catch: to get those rates, a company must offer full-time workers group health insurance, a retirement plan with at least a 50% employer match on up to 6% of pay, average pay raises of at least 3% for all but its highest-paid 10% of employees, and an extra 4.5% of wages in Social Security contributions for workers without a traditional pension. It also permanently opens a repatriation window and sends some of that new revenue to the Highway Trust Fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Full-time workers at companies that take the deal would get guaranteed average pay raises of at least 3% (the requirement covers everyone below the top 10% of earners), an offer of group health coverage, a retirement plan with employer matching, and an extra 4.5%-of-wages Social Security contribution that could either boost their future Social Security check or sit in a personal account. Companies that elect in would see their tax rate fall from as high as 35% to 10%, and multinationals could repatriate foreign earnings at 5% rather than the 35% rate minus credits that normally applied. The Highway Trust Fund would receive a dedicated transfer of repatriation revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at electing companies, and the companies

how_it_helps.text: Employers that elect the 10% rate must offer group health coverage to every full-time employee (30+ hours/week) and their dependents, with employee contributions capped by an affordability test

They must offer a defined contribution plan with a match of at least 50% of the employee's elective contributions up to 6% of pay, and pay average wage increases of at least 3% to all full-time employees outside the top 10% of earners, with special rules for commissioned and new employees

For full-time workers without a traditional pension, the employer must contribute an additional 4.5% of wages, held in a Treasury-managed fund; workers can elect to move those amounts to the Social Security trust fund to increase their future benefit, or keep them in a personal account invested in conservative, age-appropriate options

Companies electing in may repatriate both current and accumulated foreign earnings at a 5% rate on a permanent basis, and revenue from those dividends is appropriated to the Highway Account of the Highway Trust Fund
In exchange for the lower rates, electing businesses give up three major tax breaks: the domestic production activities deduction, like-kind exchanges, and installment-sale reporting

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the direct cost: the corporate rate for electing firms would drop from a top 35% to 10%, individual owners of electing pass-through businesses would pay 10% on their business income, and foreign earnings would come home taxed at 5% instead of facing the normal 35% rate less foreign tax credits. Those choices would be paid for through larger deficits or higher taxes elsewhere; the bill contained no offsetting revenue and, since it never got a committee hearing, it was never formally scored by the Joint Committee on Taxation.

drawbacks.text: The tax cuts dwarf the worker conditions in fiscal size: a 10% corporate rate, a 10% pass-through rate, and a permanent 5% repatriation holiday would sharply cut federal revenue, and the bill provided no offset — the revenue loss would land on deficits or other taxpayers

The worker benefits only bind at companies that elect the deal. Firms for which the 3% raises, 4.5% contributions, and health coverage cost more than the tax savings simply decline to elect, so most workers get nothing and the Treasury only loses revenue on firms where the deal is worth it to management
Employers may exclude employees covered by collective bargaining agreements from all the requirements, so unionized workforces would not automatically get the raises or contributions

The 3% wage requirement is measured as an average across applicable employees rather than a guarantee for each worker, and the bill's treatment of independent contractors (contractors working more than 130 days are treated as employees for the 4.5% contribution) would create compliance complications in industries that rely on contract labor

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea — trade a deep corporate tax cut for enforceable wage, health, and retirement commitments to workers — is a real bargain structure, and the worker conditions are stronger than window dressing: they are hard requirements a company must meet every year to keep the low rate. But the two sides of the trade are badly unbalanced. A 10% corporate rate was a much larger tax cut than the wage and benefit conditions would plausibly cost most large firms, the repatriation holiday was essentially unconditional once a firm elected, and the bill included no revenue offsets. It was also never scored or debated, so there is no independent estimate of whether the worker benefits would have come close to matching the revenue cost. An honest reading: good for workers at participating firms, a large and unmeasured cost to everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on April 29, 2016 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never held a hearing or markup, and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, having never left committee.

narrative.text: Rep. David McKinley (R-WV) introduced the Make America Competitive Act of 2016 on April 29, 2016
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax bills
No other member of the House — from either party — signed on as a cosponsor
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote; the bill died there when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one received anything, since nothing passed: Treasury kept the revenue that a 10% corporate rate and a 5% repatriation holiday would have forgone, and workers saw no change in wages, health coverage, or retirement benefits. The companies that would have elected into the deal — particularly multinationals sitting on offshore profits — never got the 10% and 5% rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury kept the revenue; nothing changed

for.name: Rep. David B. McKinley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on from either party, so the partisan shape of the idea was never tested on the record.

industries.industry: Large corporations and multinationals holding foreign profits
industries.note: Electing companies would have cut their tax rate from a top 35% to 10% and repatriated foreign earnings at a permanent 5% rate — the largest gains in the bill. Their gain is paid for through forgone federal revenue, though the same election would require them to deliver 3% average raises, health coverage, retirement matching, and extra Social Security contributions to their workforces.

industries.industry: Owners of pass-through businesses (partnerships, S corporations, sole proprietorships)
industries.note: Individual owners could pay 10% on their qualified business income instead of ordinary rates of up to 39.6%, if their business met the same employee-benefit conditions. As with corporations, the gain comes out of federal revenue.

Every electing employer must offer group health coverage to all full-time employees and dependents, creating a pool of newly offered employer coverage. The benefit flows to insurers' enrollments, not directly to their profits on any single policy.

Revenue from the 5% repatriation tax is appropriated to the Highway Trust Fund's Highway Account, giving road funding a dedicated new revenue stream — though one that shrinks as companies finish bringing money home.
